clue.text: Make rings out of gold piece

parts.note: or is the heraldic word for gold
a bit is a small piece

explanation.surface: A jeweller turns a gold nugget into wedding rings.
explanation.definitionFit: To orbit is to circle something repeatedly, tracing loops around it.

clue.text: Frank, dismissed, has declared

parts.note: a batsman dismissed in cricket is out
something declared has been spoken

explanation.surface: A man called Frank, sacked from his job, makes a public statement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like a man's name; it is the adjective meaning candid.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone candid who says plainly what they think.

clue.text: Well done, taking notice of bluster

indicators.note: the cheer takes the notice into its middle, holding it inside

parts.note: bravo is the cheer for a job well done
an ad is a notice in a paper

explanation.surface: Praise for a performance that turns out to be all bluster.
explanation.definitionFit: Bravado is a swaggering show of boldness, much the same as boastful bluster.

clue.text: Fellow able to get up in quarrel

indicators.note: in a down clue, getting up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: fit means able, as in fit to work

explanation.surface: A man fit enough to stand up during a row.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiff is a minor squabble or spat.

clue.text: Skinflint practised being wretched

parts.note: a skinflint is a miser
someone practised at a task is able, skilled at it

explanation.surface: A tight-fisted man rehearses being glum.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone deeply unhappy.

clue.text: Going round Aintree, he pre-selects a trip

indicators.note: a trip is a stumble, so the letters fall over into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A punter chooses a horse in advance for an outing to the races.
explanation.walkthrough: Aintree is the Liverpool racecourse that hosts the Grand National, a jumps race. 'trip' signals the anagram of HE PRE-SELECTS A.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse racing over fences at a jumps course is a steeplechaser.

clue.text: Fun events for students in tatters

definitions.meaning: student ... are charity carnivals held by British universities

explanation.surface: Students dress in ragged clothes for a charity carnival.
explanation.definitionFit: British student charity carnivals are called rags, and tatters are torn cloths or old clothes.

clue.text: Pub ethic used at checkout?

parts.note: a bar is a pub
an ethic is a moral code

explanation.surface: A pub's moral rules are applied at the till.
explanation.definitionFit: The striped label scanned at a shop till identifies the product being bought.

clue.text: Mournful poem, for example, in cathedral setting

indicators.note: the example abbreviation sits inside the name of the city

parts.note: Ely is an English city famous for its cathedral

explanation.surface: A sad poem recited in the grounds of a cathedral.
explanation.walkthrough: Ely is a small city in Cambridgeshire, England, known for its cathedral.
explanation.definitionFit: An elegy is a lament in verse, typically for the dead.

clue.text: Crying, Tom's first to get scolding

indicators.note: first means just the opening letter of Tom's is used

parts.note: an earful is a telling-off

explanation.surface: A boy named Tom bursts into tears after being told off.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone tearful is weeping or close to it.

clue.text: Absurdly taken out, from here to the Wash, say?

definitions.text: from here to the Wash, say?

indicators.note: out signals the letters are taken out of order and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A trip from somewhere to the Wash, the bay on England's east coast, ridiculously cancelled.
explanation.walkthrough: The Wash is a bay on the east coast of England, but here 'the wash' is the laundry. 'out' signals the anagram of ABSURDLY TAKEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Dirty clothes are carried from the hamper to be laundered, so the hamper is where the washing starts.

clue.text: Warning from one fencing English garden off

indicators.note: off means the letters are spoiled and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone tells a neighbour to keep out of their English garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fencing' suggests putting up a fence round the garden, but it is the sword sport; 'off' is the anagram signal, as in food gone off.
explanation.definitionFit: A fencer calls this French phrase to tell an opponent to be on guard before a bout.

clue.text: Quiet ballad in Othello, for example

parts.note: p (piano) is the musical marking for quiet
a lay is a narrative song or ballad

explanation.surface: A soft song sung during a performance of Shakespeare's Othello.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello is one of Shakespeare's dramas, written for the stage.

clue.text: Man eating very soft fish

indicators.note: the man takes the soft marking inside him, as if eating it

parts.note: a guy is a man
pp (pianissimo) is the musical marking for very soft

explanation.surface: A man eats a tender piece of fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A guppy is a small tropical freshwater fish kept in aquariums.

clue.text: Sheltered Greek island taking unknown number

parts.note: Cos (Kos) is a Greek island in the Dodecanese
y is a mathematical unknown

explanation.surface: A sheltered Greek island receives an unknown number of tourists.
explanation.definitionFit: A cosy spot is snug and protected from the weather.

clue.text: Quiet country road from Lancaster, possibly

parts.note: p (piano) is the musical marking for quiet
a lane is a narrow country road

explanation.surface: A peaceful rural road leading out of the city of Lancaster.
explanation.walkthrough: Lancaster is an English city, but here it is the Avro Lancaster, a Second World War bomber.
explanation.definitionFit: The Avro Lancaster was a British aircraft, an example of the class.

clue.text: A home that's humble

parts.note: a base is a home or headquarters

explanation.surface: A modest house is a humble home.
explanation.definitionFit: To abase someone is to humble or degrade them; both are verbs here.

clue.text: Clued-up about weekend global disaster

indicators.note: a disaster wrecks things, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone well informed about a worldwide catastrophe that struck over a weekend.
explanation.definitionFit: Being clued-up means being well informed, which is what knowing a lot amounts to.

clue.text: Indigestion, said Pepys, must be treated!

indicators.note: treating the letters works them over into a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The diarist Samuel Pepys complains of a stomach upset needing treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Pepys was a famous 17th-century English diarist.
explanation.definitionFit: Dyspepsia is the medical term for an upset stomach after eating.

clue.text: P-pipes we hear

parts.note: P is short for a coin, so these are pipes named after that coin, which we hear played

explanation.surface: A stammered word about pipes being played.
explanation.walkthrough: P is the British abbreviation for penny, so P-pipes are cheap pipes named after the coin.
explanation.definitionFit: Small cheap metal flutes are named after the coin they once cost.

clue.text: Knightly champion of a boy in anguish

indicators.note: the boy sits inside the word for anguish

parts.note: pain is anguish
a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: A gallant knight comes to the rescue of a distressed boy.
explanation.definitionFit: A paladin was one of Charlemagne's peers, hence any chivalrous champion.

clue.text: Long peninsula of West African republic?

parts.note: Iberia is the peninsula holding Spain and Portugal

explanation.surface: Asking whether a long peninsula belongs to an African state.
explanation.definitionFit: Liberia is a country on the coast of West Africa, founded as a republic.

clue.text: Piece of legislation from the beak

definitions.meaning: a draft law put before parliament

explanation.surface: A new law comes from the magistrate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beak' is British slang for a magistrate, which suits the legal surface, but here it is a bird's beak.
explanation.definitionFit: A draft law and a bird's mouthpart share the same name.

clue.text: Raises the spirits of young fellows around university

indicators.note: the boys go around the university letter, holding it inside

parts.note: boys are young fellows

explanation.surface: Being at university cheers young lads up.
explanation.definitionFit: To buoy someone up is to cheer or encourage them, keeping them afloat emotionally.

clue.text: This flower is seen in the light

definitions.text: This flower is seen in the light

parts.words: This flower is seen in the light
parts.note: the flower's name comes from an old phrase for the sun, the eye of the day, since its petals open in daylight

explanation.surface: A flower that only shows itself in sunshine.
explanation.walkthrough: The name comes from Old English for day's eye: the flower opens in daylight and closes at night.
explanation.definitionFit: This common white-petalled flower opens in daylight and closes at dusk, hence its old name.

clue.text: A pitcher?

parts.note: read as the instrument that gives an orchestra its tuning note A, not a jug or a baseball thrower

explanation.definitionFit: An orchestra tunes to the A sounded by this woodwind, so it sets the pitch.

clue.text: Soldier taking both hands of sweetheart

parts.note: a GI is an American soldier
R and L stand for right and left hands

explanation.surface: A soldier holds his sweetheart's hands in both of his.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweetheart is a girlfriend, a young woman one is courting.

clue.text: Journalist under us was habitually employed

indicators.note: in a down clue, under means the journalist comes below the other piece

parts.note: taken as written
ed is short for editor, the crossword journalist

explanation.surface: A journalist working beneath us was a regular employee.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Used' covers both being habitually done, as in used to, and being put to service.

clue.text: Former prison with the devil of a name

parts.note: old means former
nick is British slang for a prison or police station

explanation.surface: An ex-convict with a fearsome reputation.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Nick is a traditional nickname for Satan.

clue.text: Heads for holiday centres

definitions.meaning: makes for, goes to a place

explanation.surface: Tourists make their way to seaside towns.
explanation.definitionFit: Resorts as a verb means goes or turns to, and as a noun means holiday towns.

clue.text: One in a suit wearing sleeveless vest

parts.note: a singlet is a sleeveless vest
having something on means wearing it

explanation.surface: A man in a business suit with a vest underneath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suit' suggests clothing, backed by the vest; it is a suit of playing cards.
explanation.definitionFit: In card games, a lone card held in a suit is called this.

clue.text: Crisis of doctor with a morning round

indicators.note: round means turned round, so the morning abbreviation is read backwards

explanation.surface: A doctor doing the morning rounds faces an emergency.
explanation.definitionFit: A drama can mean an exciting or tense situation, a crisis.
